unit.name: PM bottleneck and product-shaped engineering
unit.description: The lecture explains how AI coding changes the bottleneck from implementation to product judgment, user feedback, and clear specifications.
unit.summary: Andrew's immediate advice is to build more things because AI has made implementation cheaper and faster [ts=303s]. Once a clear software spec can be converted into code more easily, the bottleneck shifts toward deciding what to build and writing that spec [ts=337s]. He describes a loop of building, getting user feedback, revising product judgment, and iterating toward something users love [ts=357s]. This shift may reduce the traditional engineer-to-PM ratio, and engineers who can talk with users and shape product can move unusually fast [ts=438s].

key_points.text: The advice 'go and build stuff' is stronger now because AI makes building more accessible.
When specs are easier to turn into code, deciding what to build becomes the bottleneck.
A useful product loop is build, get user feedback, revise assumptions, and iterate.
Engineer-to-PM ratios may trend downward as engineering accelerates faster than product management.
Engineers who can gather user feedback and develop product empathy are described as especially fast-moving.

kp_catalog.name: Product-management bottleneck in AI-assisted development
kp_catalog.description: When code generation accelerates implementation, deciding what to build and writing clear product specs become the limiting factors.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Product bottleneck is career/product advice, not a technical prerequisite.

kp_catalog.name: Engineer product empathy
kp_catalog.description: Engineers who can talk to users, collect feedback, and make product decisions can iterate faster in AI-assisted development workflows.
kp_catalog.importance_rationale: Andrew identifies engineers who learn to talk to users and develop empathy as among the fastest moving people he sees [ts=481s].
